title: Chinmay Sutar Hits Unbeaten 400, Only Second Indian to Reach the Mark
excerpt: The Mizoram batter made 400 not out off 517 balls against Nagaland in Sovima, passing Prithvi Shaw's 379 and finishing behind only B. B. Nimbalkar's 443 not out in Ranji Trophy history.
body:
• Chinmay Sutar scored an unbeaten 400 for Mizoram against Nagaland in a Ranji Trophy Plate match at Sovima, becoming only the second Indian to make a quadruple century in first-class cricket.
  • The 29-year-old faced 517 balls, hit 46 fours and seven sixes, and Mizoram declared at 581 for nine in the 155th over as soon as he reached the mark.
  • Sutar passed Prithvi Shaw's 379 to record the second-highest score in Ranji Trophy history, behind only B. B. Nimbalkar's unbeaten 443 in 1948-49.
  • He did it in just his second first-class match, a week after being run out for 99 on debut against Manipur.

Chinmay Sutar became only the second Indian batter to score 400 in a first-class innings on Monday, making an unbeaten 400 for Mizoram against Nagaland in a Ranji Trophy Plate group match at the Nagaland Cricket Stadium in Sovima. According to ESPNcricinfo, Sutar was unbeaten on 392 at tea and reached 400 in the 155th over, at which point Mizoram declared their first innings at 581 for nine.

An innings that kept growing

Sutar faced 517 balls and struck 46 fours and seven sixes, according to the IANS report carried by Cricketnmore. Mizoram had ended the opening day on 331 for five, then slipped to 391 for nine on the second day. Sutar was on 231 when the last batter, Lalrempuia Chhakchhuak, joined him. The pair added an unbroken 190 for the tenth wicket, with Chhakchhuak contributing 14 not out from 76 balls while Sutar farmed the strike and advanced from 231 to 400.

The next highest score in the Mizoram innings was 69. The 190-run last-wicket stand is the third-highest in Ranji Trophy history, 43 runs short of the record 233 put on by Ajay Sharma and Maninder Singh for Delhi against Mumbai in 1991-92, ESPNcricinfo reported.

Second only to Nimbalkar

By reaching 400, Sutar joined a list that has stood almost untouched in Indian cricket for more than 75 years. Bhausaheb Nimbalkar's unbeaten 443 for Maharashtra against Kathiawar in Pune in 1948-49 remains the highest first-class score by an Indian and the highest score in Ranji Trophy history. Sutar's 400 not out moves him into second place in the Ranji record books, ahead of Prithvi Shaw's 379 for Mumbai against Assam in 2022-23.

Globally, Sutar is only the tenth batter to score 400 or more in a first-class innings, a group that includes Brian Lara, who made an unbeaten 501 for Warwickshire in 1994 and 400 not out in a Test match in 2004, and Don Bradman. Pakistan's Hanif Mohammad made 499 in 1959.

A remarkable start to a first-class career

The innings came in Sutar's second first-class match. He made his Ranji Trophy debut for Mizoram in the previous week's season opener against Manipur, scoring 35 in the first innings and 99 in the second, when he was run out one short of a century as Mizoram fought back from a 68-run first-innings deficit before losing by three wickets. Across his first three first-class innings he has scored 534 runs.

Sutar, 29, previously represented Mumbai in the Vijay Hazare Trophy, the domestic 50-over competition, after strong returns in Mumbai's local leagues, ESPNcricinfo reported. In June he helped MSC Maratha Royals defend their Mumbai T20 League title, finishing that tournament with 212 runs in six innings at a strike rate close to 120, including back-to-back half-centuries at the end. Before this season he obtained a no-objection certificate from the Mumbai Cricket Association to move to Mizoram.

What it means for the match

The match itself is not over. Mizoram's declaration at 581 for nine gives Nagaland a large first innings to answer in the Plate group fixture, and the result will depend on how Nagaland bat and whether Mizoram can press for an outright win over the remaining days. Whatever the outcome, the individual record is already settled: a quadruple century, in a second first-class appearance, from a batter who a week earlier had fallen one run short of a debut hundred.

For Indian domestic cricket, the knock also puts fresh attention on the Plate group, where Mizoram and the other north-eastern sides play most of their cricket away from the national spotlight. Scores of this size are rare at any level of the first-class game. Before Monday, only one Indian had ever made one, and he did it in 1948.
